site.title: koreader-dicts — open bilingual dictionaries for e-readers
site.description: Bilingual dictionaries built by merging WordNet, the Open Multilingual Wordnet and Wiktionary, with published quality metrics.

home.title: Open bilingual dictionaries for e-readers
home.lede: Free bilingual dictionaries are poor because almost every generator uses a single source: Wiktionary. These are built by merging Wiktionary with the wordnets of the Open Multilingual Wordnet, which all share Princeton WordNet synset identifiers and can therefore be pivoted against one another. Quality metrics for every dictionary are published here — measured, not claimed.
home.noBuilds: No build output found. Run kdicts build all and then kdicts catalog.
home.howBody: Every wordnet in the Open Multilingual Wordnet maps its words onto the same Princeton WordNet 3.0 synset identifiers. Once two languages are both mapped, a dictionary between them already exists implicitly:
home.howAfter: So a pair with no direct bilingual resource anywhere — Spanish to Portuguese, say — comes out of the same pipeline as English to Portuguese. Wiktionary is then layered on top for the slang, idiom and inflected forms that wordnets lack.
home.whyTitle: Why coverage matters more than the entry count
home.whyBody: Entry counts are easy to inflate and say little. What decides whether a dictionary is useful is whether tapping a word in the middle of a book returns anything — and that depends on inflected forms as much as on headwords. A dictionary with no inflection index fails on wielded however many entries it advertises. Every pair here is measured against a frequency list, counting inflections, and the result is on its page.

downloads.title: Downloads
downloads.lede: Every dictionary is a single ZIP containing one folder. Unzip it, copy the folder onto your device, and restart KOReader. Nothing else is required, and nothing phones home.
downloads.whatYouGetBody: Each archive holds one dictionary folder with these files. You never need to open them, but it helps to know what they are:
downloads.fileIfo: Metadata: the dictionary’s name, entry count, and the attribution notice shown in KOReader’s dictionary list.
downloads.fileIdx: The index of headwords, sorted so the reader can binary-search it.
downloads.fileDict: The definitions themselves, compressed so a phone or e-reader can seek into them without unpacking the whole file.
downloads.fileSyn: The inflection index: it maps wielded to wield and geese to goose. This is what makes lookups work on real prose.
downloads.fileLicence: The licence the compilation is distributed under, and the notices each source requires.
downloads.formatBody: The definitions are already compressed inside the archive, so the gain comes almost entirely from the two plain index files. We measured the alternatives on the 21.6 MB English-to-Portuguese build:
downloads.formatDeflate: Opens on every operating system without extra software.
downloads.formatBzip2: No smaller, and not universally supported.
downloads.formatLzma: 5% smaller, five times slower, and stock Windows Explorer and macOS Archive Utility cannot open it.
downloads.formatConclusion: Five percent is not worth handing you an archive your computer refuses to open, so every download is a plain ZIP.
downloads.checksumNote: Downloads are published on GitHub Releases and rebuilt on a schedule as the upstream sources change.
downloads.listIntro: Every dictionary below downloads directly from GitHub Releases.

how.title: How it works
how.lede: What these dictionaries are made of, why they cover more than the alternatives, and how to get one onto your e-reader.
how.pivotBody: A wordnet is a database that groups words by meaning rather than by spelling. Each group of synonyms — a synset — has an identifier. The important part is that every wordnet in the Open Multilingual Wordnet reuses the identifiers from Princeton WordNet, so the same concept has the same number in every language.
how.pivotExample: That means the moment two languages are both mapped, a dictionary between them already exists. It has simply never been written down. Spanish to Portuguese needs no Spanish-Portuguese resource at all — only the two wordnets and a configuration file.
how.pivotWhy: A generator that only reads Wiktionary cannot do this, because it needs a direct translation table to exist, and for most language pairs one does not.
how.layer1Body: Supplies the concepts, the sense structure, the English definitions and the usage examples. It also provides hand-curated irregular forms — went belongs to go, and no rule can derive that.
how.layer2Body: Supplies the words in your language, attached to those same concepts. This is where the translations come from.
how.layer3Body: Layered on top for what wordnets structurally lack: slang, idiom, proper nouns, recent vocabulary, pronunciation, and above all the inflection tables.
how.inflectionBody: Books do not contain headwords. They contain wielded, geese, running. A dictionary that only indexes wield, goose and run will report “not found” for a word it actually knows. Every dictionary here ships a separate inflection index mapping hundreds of thousands of inflected forms back to their entry, and the coverage figures on each dictionary’s page count those forms.
how.honestBody: Roughly four entries in ten have a definition but no translation: the wordnet knows the concept and your language has no single word for it. Those are shipped anyway, because a definition still helps, and they are counted separately in every metric rather than folded into the entry total. Pairs that do not involve English ship without an inflection index: the inflection rules are English-only.

how.kindleTitle: Getting KOReader onto a Kindle first
how.kindleBody: These dictionaries are for KOReader, not for the Kindle’s built-in reader. KOReader can be installed on any jailbroken Kindle: extract its release archive so that the koreader and extensions folders sit at the root of the Kindle’s USB drive, eject the device, and launch the new entry that appears in your library. The official guide covers each firmware version.
how.kindleWarning: Jailbreaking is done at your own risk, and the official documentation is the authority on the procedure for your firmware — not this page.
